items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite being ...), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is a possessive noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the city’s gold leaf)
items.passage: Kanazawa, Japan, manufactures nearly all of the country’s gold leaf, which artisans produce by repeatedly hammering gold between sheets of specially treated paper. Despite being hundreds of times thinner than a human hair, ______ years of exposure to sunlight and rainfall on the exteriors of temples and shrines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the city produces gold leaf that is sturdy enough to withstand
the city’s gold leaf is sturdy enough to withstand
it is the city’s gold leaf that is sturdy enough to withstand
the gold leaf’s sturdiness allows it to withstand
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Despite being hundreds of times thinner than a human hair,” describes something extremely thin: the gold leaf. Choice B places “the city’s gold leaf” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the gold leaf, though thin, is sturdy enough to withstand years of sunlight and rainfall. The possessive “the city’s” only tells whose gold leaf it is; the subject is “gold leaf.”

A.why_wrong: The subject is “the city,” so the sentence illogically says that the city is hundreds of times thinner than a human hair.

C.why_wrong: The sentence begins with “it is,” so the opening phrase has nothing to describe; “the city’s gold leaf” appears only inside the “it is ... that” frame.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the gold leaf’s sturdiness,” not the gold leaf, so the sentence illogically says that sturdiness is hundreds of times thinner than a human hair.

items.notes: Subject: Kanazawa gold leaf (arts and crafts). Facts kept general and known (Kanazawa makes nearly all of Japan’s gold leaf, beaten between treated paper to about 0.1 micrometer, several hundred times thinner than a hair; used on temple exteriors). Band 7 as 37e5c794 (3.16, the only band-7 prep-gerund official): property opener (Despite being + thickness), right subject a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (band7 section 3.7: 3 of 5 band-7 R3 keys work this way), W uses that obvious noun (the city), E carries the key’s own noun phrase inside the cleft, P/N subject is the hammering. A student drilled to reject possessive subjects (recipe P) is drawn away from the key. All options grammatical on their own, 9 to 12 words; key not the longest. Reviewer: D was the artisans’ hammering (killed by one obvious fact); it is now the possessive of the obvious noun, as the P option of 37e5c794 (commercial plastics’ two associated problems), so B and D both open with a possessive built on gold leaf and the student must find the head noun.

fixes: D hardened from “the artisans’ hammering makes the leaf” (killed by one obvious fact) to the possessive of the obvious noun, “the gold leaf’s sturdiness allows it to withstand,” as 37e5c794; why_wrong and notes updated
review.note: Key seen in the first structure dump before the blind solve (blind solve compromised). FSS: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); real subjects with general known facts, no invented names, nothing attributed to a real person or organisation beyond common knowledge; every option tested in the full sentence, exactly one grammatical.

band7.why: Modelled on the only band-7 prep-gerund official, 37e5c794: property opener (Despite being + thinness), key a possessive noun phrase built on the obvious noun (the city’s gold leaf), and after the reviewer fix a P distractor that is the possessive of that same noun (the gold leaf’s sturdiness), plus a cleft carrying the key’s noun phrase (E) and the city as subject (W). A student who rejects possessive subjects on sight loses the key; one who matches nouns is drawn to C and D. One defensible answer by head-noun logic.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Mastering programming languages ...), passage-final blank; the person is the right subject
items.passage: In 1955, Annie Easley joined the agency that would become NASA as a “human computer,” one of the employees who performed complex calculations by hand. Mastering programming languages as electronic computers gradually took over that work, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Easley’s code for the Centaur rocket stage has helped launch numerous satellites and space probes.
the Centaur rocket stage relied on code that Easley wrote to launch numerous satellites and space probes.
it was Easley who wrote code for the Centaur rocket stage, which has launched numerous satellites and space probes.
Easley later wrote code for the Centaur rocket stage, which has launched numerous satellites and space probes.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Mastering programming languages as electronic computers gradually took over that work,” describes a person who learned to program: Annie Easley. Choice D places “Easley” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Easley mastered programming languages and later wrote code for the Centaur rocket stage.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “Easley’s code,” not Easley, so the sentence illogically says that the code mastered programming languages.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “the Centaur rocket stage,” so the sentence illogically says that a rocket stage mastered programming languages.

C.why_wrong: The sentence begins with “it was,” so the opening phrase is left with nothing to describe; Easley appears only inside the “it was ... who” frame.

items.notes: Subject: Annie Easley, NACA/NASA Lewis human computer from 1955 who became a programmer; Centaur upper stage (science and technology). Known facts kept general. Band 6 as 9df6da04 (3.14) and dab8b8ee (3.5): plain agent key after an -ing opener, passage-final full-sentence options, three different recipes (P, W, E). Key 17 words, C is longer (18).

review.note: FSS: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); real subjects with general known facts, no invented names, nothing attributed to a real person or organisation beyond common knowledge; every option tested in the full sentence, exactly one grammatical.

band7.why: Plain agent key after an -ing opener with P, W and E distractors, as band-6 9df6da04 and dab8b8ee; the right subject is the obvious noun (Easley), so it does not reach the band-7 setting (property opener, noun-phrase key).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: verb of a relative clause whose antecedent is plural (workers who), with a concessive interrupter holding a singular possessive and a singular verb
items.passage: Before electric streetlights became widespread, London depended on lamplighters to maintain its gas lamps. Nineteenth-century accounts describe workers who, though each one’s nightly route was a circuit of dozens of lamps distributed across several neighborhoods, ______ expected to illuminate every lamp along it before complete darkness descended.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the verb of the relative clause “who ... expected to illuminate every lamp along it,” and “who” refers to the plural noun “workers.” The plural verb “were” agrees with it. The interrupter “though each one’s nightly route was a circuit of dozens of lamps distributed across several neighborhoods” does not change the subject of “who.”

B.why_wrong: “Was” is singular; it agrees with “each one’s nightly route” inside the interrupter, not with “workers,” the antecedent of “who.”

C.why_wrong: “Is” is singular and so does not agree with the plural antecedent “workers.”

D.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and so does not agree with the plural antecedent “workers.”

items.notes: Subject (reviewer replacement; the 1930 Plains Indian Sign Language council joined about 8 live sign-language items): nineteenth-century London lamplighters and their nightly routes (social science, history). Known facts kept general; no named source. Band 6 as ee4aa2aa (relative-clause verb with a plural antecedent) plus a 16-word interrupter between who and the blank carrying a singular possessive (each one’s), a singular head (route) and a singular finite verb (was), so the singular options sound right twice. Options are the be-family set: wrong number in three tenses.

fixes: subject replaced: the 1930 Plains Indian Sign Language council joined a crowded sign-language theme (about 8 live items); now nineteenth-century London lamplighters, same frame (plural antecedent of who, 16-word concessive interrupter with singular possessive and singular verb was); explanation and why_wrong rewritten; claimed in claims.txt
review.note: FSS: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); real subjects with general known facts, no invented names, nothing attributed to a real person or organisation beyond common knowledge; every option tested in the full sentence, exactly one grammatical.

band7.why: Relative-clause verb with a plural antecedent next to who, as band-6 ee4aa2aa, made harder by a 16-word concessive interrupter with a singular possessive and its own singular verb (was); the band-7 R1_rel_poss setting (a possessor of the other number before the head) is not used.

items.subtype: Possessive determiner before its antecedent (Because ______ flowers ..., the plant), plural noun right after the blank
items.passage: For most of the year, the night-blooming cereus (Peniocereus greggii) is an inconspicuous cactus of the Sonoran Desert. Because ______ fragrant white flowers remain open for only a single night, the plant attracts crowds of spectators to a botanical garden in Tucson, Arizona, on the evening when horticulturists predict the buds will open.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The flowers belong to the plant, the night-blooming cereus, which is named again right after the pronoun as “the plant.” That noun is singular, as the singular verb “attracts” shows, so the singular possessive determiner “its” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “Their” is plural; it seems to fit the plural “flowers” that follows, but the flowers belong to the singular “plant,” the night-blooming cereus.

B.why_wrong: “They’re” means “they are,” which makes no sense before “fragrant white flowers,” and it is plural.

D.why_wrong: “It’s” means “it is” or “it has,” not the possessive “its.”

items.notes: Subject: night-blooming cereus, Peniocereus greggii, whose flowers open for one night and draw crowds to a Tucson garden on bloom night (natural science). Known facts kept general. Band 6 as 872a002e (3.22): the referent is named in the first sentence and again 10 words after the determiner (the plant), with the plural noun flowers right after the blank; 2 x 2 grid of its/their and contractions. No other plural noun in the passage can own the flowers.

review.note: FSS: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); real subjects with general known facts, no invented names, nothing attributed to a real person or organisation beyond common knowledge; every option tested in the full sentence, exactly one grammatical.

band7.why: Determiner before its antecedent (the plant) with a plural noun right after the blank, the setting of band-7 0bcb4417, but the cereus is named as a singular in the first sentence and the plant 10 words later, so the antecedent is easier to find than in 0bcb4417; a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family: plural head (domes) behind a long appositive with singular nouns and its own singular verb; 26 words after the blank
items.passage: The onion-shaped domes of the Church of the Transfiguration, an elaborate wooden church that was constructed in 1714 on Kizhi Island in Russia’s Lake Onega, ______ covered with thousands of hand-cut aspen shingles that gradually weather to a silvery sheen, making the structure appear from a distance to be sheathed in metal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun “domes,” so the plural verb “are” is needed. Everything between “domes” and the blank, “of the Church of the Transfiguration, an elaborate wooden church that was constructed in 1714 on Kizhi Island in Russia’s Lake Onega,” describes the church and does not change the number of the subject.

A.why_wrong: “Is” is singular; it seems to agree with “the Church of the Transfiguration” or “an elaborate wooden church,” but the subject is the plural “domes.”

C.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and echoes “was constructed” inside the appositive, but the subject is the plural “domes.”

D.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and so does not agree with the plural subject “domes.”

items.notes: Subject (reviewer replacement; the Chand Baori was a second Indian stepwell after live FSS w1b4_22, Rani ki Vav): onion domes of the Church of the Transfiguration, Kizhi Island, Lake Onega, Russia (1714), covered with aspen shingles that weather to silver (history and architecture). Known facts kept general. Band 7 settings (band7 section 5, R1_be): plural head with no number word, behind singular nouns as dc645172 (3.3); the intervener has its own singular finite verb (was constructed); singular attractors Church, Transfiguration, church, Kizhi Island, Lake Onega (5); head to blank 22 words; 26 run words after the blank; run 52 words. Options wrong number in three tenses, no right-number distractor.

fixes: subject replaced: the Chand Baori was a second Indian stepwell after live FSS w1b4_22 (Rani ki Vav); now the domes of Kizhi’s Church of the Transfiguration, same band-7 settings (plural head, 5 singular attractors, own singular verb was constructed, 26 words after the blank); claimed in claims.txt
review.note: FSS: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); real subjects with general known facts, no invented names, nothing attributed to a real person or organisation beyond common knowledge; every option tested in the full sentence, exactly one grammatical.

band7.why: Band-7 R1_be settings (band7 section 5) on the new text: plural head with no number word (domes) behind 5 singular attractors and an appositive relative clause with its own singular verb (was constructed), head 22 words before the blank, 26 run words after it, options wrong number in three tenses as dc645172.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, compound subject of two singular nouns (Its first sting ... and its second ...), the second with a relative clause holding singular verbs
items.passage: The jewel wasp (Ampulex compressa) subdues cockroaches without killing them. Its first sting, delivered to a cockroach’s thorax, and its second, which is injected into a region of the brain that regulates the motivation to walk, ______ the considerably larger insect sufficiently docile to be guided by an antenna into the wasp’s burrow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is compound: “Its first sting ... and its second” names two stings joined by “and,” so it is plural and takes the plural verb “leave.” The phrases and clauses describing each sting, including “which is injected” and “that regulates,” do not change the number of the subject.

A.why_wrong: “Leaves” is singular; it seems to agree with the nearby “its second” or “a region of the brain,” but two stings joined by “and” form a plural subject.

B.why_wrong: “Is leaving” is singular and so does not agree with the plural compound subject.

C.why_wrong: “Has left” is singular and so does not agree with the plural compound subject.

items.notes: Subject: jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa, which stings a cockroach first in the thorax and then in the brain and leads it by an antenna to its burrow (natural science). Known facts kept general. Band 7 settings (band7 section 5, R1_quant_compound and R1): compound of two singular nouns as c7cb5186, the second elided (its second) and followed by a relative clause with two singular finite verbs (is injected, regulates); singular nouns thorax, region, brain, motivation between; 16 run words after the blank; plural key (half of band-7 R1 keys are plural).

review.note: FSS: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); real subjects with general known facts, no invented names, nothing attributed to a real person or organisation beyond common knowledge; every option tested in the full sentence, exactly one grammatical.

band7.why: Compound of two singular nouns as c7cb5186, with the second conjunct elided (its second) and followed by a relative clause holding two singular verbs (is injected, regulates); five singular nouns between, 28 words from the first head to the blank, 16 run words after it.

items.subtype: Personal pronoun number: singular thing (the harp) with plural nouns (audiences, symphony orchestras, albums) between it and the pronoun
items.passage: Detroit-born musician Dorothy Ashby helped establish the harp as a jazz instrument during the 1950s and 1960s. Audiences at the time associated the harp primarily with symphony orchestras, but on a series of acclaimed albums, Ashby demonstrated that ______ could accommodate the rapid, intricate melodies of bebop.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “the harp,” the instrument Ashby played and the topic of the passage. “The harp” is singular, so the singular pronoun “it” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “They” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular antecedent “the harp”; it seems to point to the nearby plural “symphony orchestras.”

B.why_wrong: “This” is ambiguous here; it could point to the idea in the previous clause rather than clearly to the harp.

D.why_wrong: “Those” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular antecedent “the harp.”

items.notes: Subject: Dorothy Ashby, Detroit jazz harpist of the 1950s and 1960s (arts, music). Known facts kept general. Medium as b85c19ed (2.15) and c52652c9 (2.3): singular antecedent with plural nouns (Audiences, symphony orchestras, albums) between it and the pronoun; options it, they, those, and this (CB marks this as ambiguous, 908a76b8). One and she left out: generic one could be read as a person, and she as Ashby herself.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor plus plural noun (the writer’s short stories), possessor named only in the previous sentence
items.passage: Dorothy West, who began publishing fiction as a teenager during the Harlem Renaissance, is best remembered for her novels The Living Is Easy (1948) and The Wedding (1995). For nearly two decades, however, many of the ______ were published in the New York Daily News, a newspaper with an enormous readership.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The stories belong to one writer, Dorothy West, so the singular possessive “writer’s” is needed. “Many of the” shows that more than one story is meant, and nothing belongs to the stories, so the plain plural “stories” is correct.

B.why_wrong: “Writers” has no apostrophe, so it does not show that the stories belong to the writer.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Story’s” is possessive, but nothing belongs to the stories; the plain plural “stories” is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Writers’” is a plural possessive, but the stories belong to one writer, Dorothy West.

items.notes: Subject: Dorothy West, Harlem Renaissance writer, whose short stories ran in the New York Daily News for about two decades (literature). Known facts kept general. Medium as 819c443d (2.24, the provocative author’s political writings): two-slot grid, partial; the possessor is a noun standing for the person named in the previous sentence. Number cues: Dorothy West (one writer), many of the (plural stories). No plural writers in the passage, so writers’ has no possible referent.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: singular head (book) behind a title ending in a plural noun and a participial phrase with a plural noun
items.passage: During the 1970s, urbanist William H. Whyte recorded pedestrian activity in New York City’s plazas and parks with time-lapse cameras. His 1980 book The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces, based on years of this footage, ______ that people tend to congregate where other people have already gathered.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “book” (“His 1980 book The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces”), so the singular verb “argues” is needed. The plural nouns “Spaces” and “years” sit between the subject and the blank but do not change its number.

A.why_wrong: “Argue” is plural; it seems to agree with “Spaces” or “years,” but the subject is the singular “book.”

C.why_wrong: “Are arguing” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “book.”

D.why_wrong: “Have argued” is plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject “book.”

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After publishing ...), mid-sentence blank; the person is the right subject
items.passage: In 1944, Frank Yerby received an O. Henry Award for “Health Card,” a short story confronting racial discrimination in the military. After publishing several such stories, ______ a sweeping romance set in antebellum New Orleans, The Foxes of Harrow (1946), which sold more than a million copies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: popular historical fiction became Yerby’s focus, beginning with
Yerby’s turn to popular historical fiction began with
it was popular historical fiction that Yerby turned to, beginning with
Yerby turned to popular historical fiction, beginning with
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “After publishing several such stories,” describes the person who published them: Frank Yerby. Choice D places “Yerby” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Yerby published the stories and then turned to popular historical fiction.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “popular historical fiction,” so the sentence illogically says that fiction published several short stories.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “Yerby’s turn,” not Yerby, so the sentence illogically says that a turn published several short stories.

C.why_wrong: The sentence begins with “it was,” so the opening phrase is left with nothing to describe; Yerby appears only inside the “it was ... that” frame.

items.notes: Subject: Frank Yerby, O. Henry Award for Health Card (1944), then The Foxes of Harrow (1946), the first million-selling novel by an African American writer (literature). items.subtype: Tense: simple past for a dated event (in 1365) inside a relative clause, with present-tense verbs around it
items.passage: Historians of medieval Southeast Asia rely extensively on the Nagarakretagama, a lengthy Old Javanese poem that the Buddhist official Mpu Prapanca ______ in 1365 to glorify King Hayam Wuruk. The poem also enumerates dozens of territories reportedly paying tribute to his Majapahit Empire across the Indonesian archipelago.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The poet finished the poem at a specific time in the past, “in 1365,” so the simple past “completed” is correct. The present-tense verbs “rely” and “enumerates” describe how the poem is used and what it contains today, not when it was written.

A.recipe: present simple where another tense is needed
A.why_wrong: “Completes” is the present tense, but the poem was finished in 1365.

B.why_wrong: “Is completing” describes an action happening now, which does not fit an event dated to 1365.

D.recipe: present simple or present perfect where another tense is needed
D.why_wrong: “Has completed” is the present perfect, which is not used with a specific past date such as “in 1365.”

items.notes: Subject: Mpu Prapanca’s Nagarakretagama (1365), eulogy of Hayam Wuruk listing Majapahit tributaries (history). Known facts kept general. Medium as 67614549 (2.12): the dated past sits inside a present-tense frame (rely, lists) so the present forms tempt; distractors present, present progressive, present perfect. Only one tense fits the date.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate (published ... and ______), split by a dash pair
items.passage: In 1926, Turkish novelist Halide Edib published her memoirs in English—a language she had acquired as a student at the American College for Girls in Istanbul—and ______ them in 1928 with a sequel chronicling her experiences during the nationalist struggle that established modern Turkey.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the second verb of the compound predicate that begins “Halide Edib published her memoirs”: she published them “and followed them” with a sequel. “Followed” is a finite past-tense verb, parallel with “published.” The dash pair only adds information about English and does not change the structure.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: “Following” is a participle, so “and following them” has no finite verb to match “published.”

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
C.why_wrong: “To follow” is an infinitive, so “and to follow them” has no finite verb to match “published.”

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having followed” is a participle phrase, so “and having followed them” has no finite verb to match “published.”

items.notes: Subject: Halide Edib, Memoirs of Halide Edib (1926) in English and The Turkish Ordeal (1928); American College for Girls, Istanbul (literature). Known facts kept general. Medium as b74f676f (2.1): compound predicate split by a closed em dash pair; canonical options finite, -ing, to + base, having + participle.
